summary: Chau Tran frames the central question for AI builders as whether to build workflows or agents. Workflows orchestrate LLMs and tools through predefined code paths—either imperative code or declarative graphs—providing predictability, lower cost and latency, easier debugging, and human control, likened to a Toyota. Agents let LLMs dynamically direct their own processes through a plan-execute-observe loop; they are more open-ended and benefit from improving LLM capabilities but are higher cost and latency and can unpredictably fail, likened to a Tesla. The pivotal reframing is that an agent takes a task and generates a workflow to achieve it, revealing four synergies: golden workflows can evaluate agents by comparing step traces; golden workflow libraries can train agents; agents can generate workflows for workflow-building platforms (how Glean agents work); and agents serve as workflow discovery engines whose successful runs become saved workflows and training data. Enterprise-aware AGI still needs onboarding because company-specific protocols produce great outputs. Two training approaches are compared. Fine-tuning (SFT/RLHF) is like building custom hardware—optimized for stable, generalized behaviors where ground truth doesn't change, but costly to update and poorly suited for per-team personalization. Dynamic prompting through search is like writing software—less optimized but flexible, better for customized behaviors and rapidly changing requirements, and offers interpretability by exposing the exact examples affecting outputs. Building Workflow Search resembles document search with two components: textual similarity (hybrid search using lexical, vector embeddings, reranking, late interaction) and authoritiveness signals from a knowledge graph (creator proximity, success rate, social signals like Slack posts). In enterprise settings, pure text similarity is insufficient because hundreds of similar-looking workflows exist; authoritiveness signals, drawn from recommender system techniques, are hard to encode directly into an LLM, necessitating a separate search system. A Q&A on data requirements for fine-tuning with RLVR defers to task-specific out-of-distribution considerations.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Workflows vs Agents: Definitions and Tradeoffs
sections.summary: Defines workflows as systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths (imperative code or declarative graphs), providing structure, predictability, lower cost and latency, and easier debugging. Defines agents as systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes through a plan-execute-observe loop, offering flexibility and open-ended problem-solving at higher cost and latency. Uses the Toyota vs Tesla analogy to highlight predictability vs brilliance-with-occasional-failure.

sections.title: Synergies Between Workflows and Agents
sections.summary: Reframes agents as systems that take a task and generate a workflow. Identifies four synergies: (1) workflows as evaluation for agents by comparing step traces to golden workflows, (2) golden workflow libraries as training data for agents, (3) agents generating workflows for workflow-building platforms (how Glean agents work), and (4) agents as workflow discovery engines that save successful runs as future training data. Discusses enterprise-aware AGI still needing company onboarding.

sections.title: Training Agents with Task-to-Workflow Data
sections.summary: Presents two training approaches. Fine-tuning (SFT and RLHF) learns well from large datasets but forks the frontier LLM, requires retraining when tools or processes change, and poorly supports personalization. Dynamic prompting through search retrieves similar task-workflow pairs at runtime and feeds them as examples, offering a spectrum of determinism (high-confidence matches) and creativity (no match). Competitor analysis example illustrates composed workflow generation.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning vs Dynamic Prompting Comparison and Building Workflow Search
sections.summary: Compares the two approaches: fine-tuning is like building custom hardware—optimized for stable, generalized behaviors but costly to change; dynamic prompting with search is like writing software—less optimized but flexible and interpretable, better for customized behaviors and rapidly changing requirements. Describes how to build Workflow Search: it resembles document search with two components—textual similarity (hybrid search with lexical, vector embeddings, reranking, late interaction) and authoritiveness signals from a knowledge graph (creator proximity, success rate, social signals). In enterprise settings, pure text similarity is insufficient because many similar-looking workflows exist; authoritiveness signals from recommender system techniques are hard to encode into an LLM, requiring a separate search system. Closes with key takeaways and a Q&A on fine-tuning data requirements with RLVR.

demonstrations: Glean agents generate workflows from natural language task descriptions, allowing users to edit or modify the proposed steps

Competitor analysis example: retrieving workflows for analyzing competitors and finding recent customer calls, then composing a new workflow that reads customer calls, extracts competitors, and runs analysis for each
limitations: Fine-tuning creates a fork from the frontier LLM, requiring retraining when newer models appear
